extracted.intended_audience: criminal investigators, judges, lawyers, and legal psychologists assessing witness testimony
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for legal practitioners on assessing the reliability and character of witness statements by analysing imagination, memory, speech, intellectual processes, subconscious acts, and situational factors that affect testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapidity of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The rapidity of speech of a witness indicates how much he has thought on a question and is certain what he is going to say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid, fluent delivery suggests conviction and easy recall; slow, hesitant, stuttering speech suggests uncertainty, active reconstruction, or consideration of alternatives. Public speakers (judges, prosecutors, defense counsel) show the same pattern. Stenographers confirm this observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of slow speech despite accurate memory
rubrics_metrics.description: It is conceivable that a person trying to remember an event accurately will speak slowly and stutteringly, or at least with hesitation at the moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rigidly equate slow speech with falsity — slow delivery can reflect cautious accurate recollection or efforts to avoid contradiction. Consider context and whether the witness is deliberating or uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination and substitutional adequacy of images
rubrics_metrics.description: The things witnesses tell us have formerly existed in their imaginations, and the 'how' of this existence determines in a large degree the 'quale' of what they offer us. Substitutional adequacy of images varies with familiarity (e.g., one can imagine one's own dog accurately, Bismarck's dog fairly well, Alcibiades' dog poorly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the representativeness of a witness’s mental images by considering how that image was formed (direct perception, pictorial knowledge, hearsay). Where the witness lacks firsthand perceptual basis, expect poorer reliability. Use knowledge of stimulus conditions to value correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain conditions under which images were obtained
rubrics_metrics.description: When we speak with a witness we rarely know the conditions under which he has obtained his images, and we learn them only from him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly elicit and evaluate the source and conditions of a witness's images (direct observation, picture, story, imagination). The reliability of the testimony depends on these conditions; the observer must probe them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation never identical with object; individual standards vary
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation can never be identical with its object; people possess an innate corrective with which he assigns proper place to image and object, but not all people possess an identical standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for inevitable distortions between perception/representation and reality and for individual differences in how images are interpreted. Do not expect perfect correspondence; instead, evaluate witness reliability relative to their personal standard and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory alteration by preference or reconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: If we have perceived something which did not appear to us altogether correct, we improve the thing in imagination and later remember the improved (altered) version rather than the actual form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for idealization or 'improvement' over repeated recall (e.g., changing colors, features). Repeated imaginings can fix an altered version as memory; question discrepancies and look for signs of progressive change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of first image from hearsay and difficult correction
rubrics_metrics.description: When one first imagines an event from scant news (e.g., a telegraphic account), an initial image may be vivid though false, and later corrections often fail; the first image may remain most vigorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of early-formed imaginative constructions (press reports, rumors) that persist and contaminate actual recollection despite correction attempts. Trace exposure to prior accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garrulity and excessive sequential recall as an unreliability sign
rubrics_metrics.description: The reproduction of images depends on sequence; this leads to the garrulity of children, old men, and uneducated people, who present the whole complex of relations and drive judges to despair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive, unfocused narrative that supplies every associated image (verbosity) often distracts from important facts and may indicate poor selective thought. Prefer concise protocols; look for omission of what is directly illuminating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value concision in protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Good protocols are almost always comparatively short; the real thinker will be chary of words and retain only those images most closely related to his immediate purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek brevity and relevance in recorded statements; long, diffuse accounts increase risk of irrelevant or misleading detail entering the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of representing and recalling movement and sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A successive series of images is not a represented succession; movement is difficult to represent or imagine and cannot be recalled point-by-point reliably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect accurate recall of continuous movement or precise sequencing; witnesses often can imagine single instants but not the succession. Question detailed accounts of movement sequences and corroborate with other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muscular innervation indicates movement imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The representation of movement awakens muscle-movement; when movement is thought of, the awakening of the muscular sense is frequently obvious and indicates the witness is trying to remember what he has seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe slight physical movements (hand gestures, tensing) when witnesses describe actions — these may signal genuine recollective effort about movement. Use behavioral cues as corroborative, not definitive, evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings and pictures render only single instants
rubrics_metrics.description: A picture can never give us a movement, but only a single state within that movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat drawings or photographs as capturing instants rather than dynamics; avoid inferring continuous action from static images without other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time effects on image construction and vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the time needed to construct an image and the time during which an image lasts with uniform vividness; Exner observed uniform vividness lasts hardly a second and the image then fades in waves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider when a recall was made relative to the event and the number of times it has been recalled; images fade and change non-uniformly. Account for rapid fading of content and wave-like loss when evaluating testimony immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated recall causes progressive alteration of images
rubrics_metrics.description: With progressive repetition of the recall of an image its content is not equally capable of reproduction; new images will tend in some definite direction (progressively bigger or smaller, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that successive recalls can systematically bias and alter details; a witness may become more definite or shift details with repeated questioning. Avoid leading repetition that may create conviction where none existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness persuasion during examination
rubrics_metrics.description: We frequently observe that a witness persuades himself into the belief of some definite idea in the course of his examination, inasmuch as with regard to some matter he says more and more definite things at the end than at the beginning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to growing confidence or increased definiteness over the course of questioning as a potential product of recall drift or suggestion; corroborate late-emerging specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on apprehending others' images
rubrics_metrics.description: How other people construct their ideas we do not know; there is difficulty in apprehending the ideas or images of other people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept epistemic limits — you cannot directly access another's mental image. Use cross-examination, corroboration, and probing of source and conditions to infer reliability rather than presuming identical perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge intelligence by handling of simple facts
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover what kind of mind a person has, start with some simple fact which has arisen in the case and try to discover what the witness will do with it — the manner, intensity, and direction of speculation reveal intelligence and objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple, concrete questions drawn from case material to test reasoning and objectivity. A witness's ability to handle basic facts reveals their capacity for sound inference; avoid tests requiring elaborate abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume thought behind repeated action
rubrics_metrics.description: The lawyer’s greatest mistake is presupposing that whoever has done anything has also thought about doing it; many people repeat actions without underlying reasoned thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inferring motive or deliberate thought simply from repeated conduct; seek direct evidence of intent or deliberation rather than assuming it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of authority, school, and media (common-source conformity)
rubrics_metrics.description: People apperceive, think, and feel as school, newspaper, and theater teach them; many witnesses present stories dependent upon opinion of some other element, and unanimity may have a single source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether apparent unanimity among witnesses stems from a common source (media, authority, prior consultation). Where a common source is found, unanimity is an unreliable means of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbol vs symbolized and promptness of response
rubrics_metrics.description: The symbol recalls its object more quickly than the object the symbol; name and word recall more quickly, reliably, and energetically the objects they stand for than do the objects their symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use promptness of response as an indicator but interpret carefully: delayed naming but immediate recognition (or vice versa) can be normal psychological variation and not indicative of deceit. Consider relationship between names, symbols, and percepts in assessing response latency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychic capacity varies with time of day
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychical capacity increases from morning to noon, drops until five o’clock, then increases until nine in the evening and finally sinks until midnight; the period between noon and five is often not favorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, schedule important examinations at times when the individual is optimally alert; be cautious interpreting statements given during commonly low periods (post-noon to late afternoon). Account for individual variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance and limits of unconscious operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconscious operations are significant: we perform unconsciously things that are deeply habitual; complex unconscious actions are possible given familiar conditions, but limits exist (novel acts do not become unconscious immediately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe unconscious habitual behavior (automatic actions, slips) to infer routine competence or character, but recognize the boundary: recently performed or novel tasks are unlikely to be unconscious. Use observation of habitual, environment-dependent acts as supplemental evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multitask inhibition and feasibility of simultaneous acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Idea A may get on with idea B and even idea C; but B and C together may make A impossible — only the summation of their inhibition could serve to exclude A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims of having done multiple simultaneous things, consider interference effects: identify plausible combinations of tasks and whether combined attentional demands would inhibit certain recollections or actions. Use this to approximate what could have been done unconsciously versus consciously.
